- If sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate and should reduce forecast slope or add downward bias.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and price is trending down, model often underestimates the drop — increase forecast downward momentum.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >5% from prior day), model frequently overshoots and continues upward — cap forecast at 1–2% above peak or add early reversal signal.
- When sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish, model often fails to adjust quickly — apply lag correction: delay forecast drop by 1–2 days or reduce slope.
- Mean reversion is strong in 30-day horizon — if forecast is >65% above 30-day moving average, reduce by 1–2% per day until convergence.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “0.00” or “0.33” (neutral/weak), model often fails to capture volatility — increase forecast volatility or add 1–2% buffer for downside risk.
- Forecast should not be linear — if sentiment shows strong trend reversal, model should curve downward or upward with exponential decay to reflect sentiment momentum.
